title: Make-Believe Media
author: Michael Parenti
desc: Cine y televisión al servicio de la clase dominante.
tesis: Hollywood y la televisión no son simple entretenimiento — son la fábrica de ideología más eficiente del mundo. Parenti analiza cómo el cine y la TV presentan sistemáticamente al capitalismo como natural, al individualismo como virtud, a los ricos como héroes, a los trabajadores como invisibles o peligrosos, y a los movimientos sociales como amenazas. Los medios de ficción son tan políticos como los noticieros — solo que su propaganda es más efectiva porque no parece propaganda.
ideas: El cine de Hollywood refuerza la ideología dominante: individualismo heroico, consumismo como felicidad, orden social como dado natural.
Los trabajadores son invisibilizados o caricaturizados en la ficción; los empresarios son los héroes de la narrativa cultural.
La ficción es más eficaz como propaganda que las noticias porque la audiencia baja la guardia crítica cuando se 'entretiene'.
contexto: Publicado en 1986 (primera edición), contemporáneo de Manufacturing Consent de Chomsky/Herman (1988). Parenti analiza cómo los medios de comunicación estadounidenses no informan sino que manufacturan la visión del mundo que conviene al poder corporativo. Cada edición actualizada incluye nuevos ejemplos de manipulación.

conexiones.razon: Inventing Reality analiza los medios informativos; Make-Believe Media analiza los medios de ficción — dos brazos del mismo sistema.
The Culture Struggle profundiza el análisis de la cultura como campo de batalla ideológico.

Even more notorious is D. W. Griffith's silent era Birth of a Nation (1915), which paints a frightening picture of the Reconstruction period, complete with corrupt and villainous Black legislators, arrogant mulattoes who treat old Confederates with bruising insolence, and leering Black soldiers who lust after White women.

The Real Glory borra la guerra en Filipinas

In The Real Glory (1939) Gary Cooper plays an Army doctor who solves all the medical and military problems in the Philippine islands in the wake of the Spanish-American War. The movie offers not a hint of why the U.S. Army was in the Philippines, and nothing about how U.S. forces invaded

HUAC inicia la cacería en Hollywood

After the war in 1947 and again in 1951, the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC) launched a full-blown investigative campaign against "Communist influence" in Hollywood. HUAC had a number of goals: First: expose movies that were "Communistic" or "sympathetic to the Communist point of view."
Ch. The Media Fight the Red Menace
Lista negra contra dos mil artistas

In the end, HUAC blacklisted or "graylisted" nearly two thousand artists in the motion picture, radio, and television industries. ... Meantime, [led by its president Ronald Reagan] the Screen Actors Guild [SAG] joined the "Crusade for Freedom," a counterattack against "communism."

Salt of the Earth contra el cine de clase

One of the most uncompromising and politically advanced films about class struggle ever made is an American one. Salt of the Earth (1954). It is based on a real-life 1951-52 strike led by Mexican-American workers against a zinc mine in New Mexico.
Ch. Blue-Collar Blues
On the Waterfront culpa al sindicato

The Oscar-winning film On the Waterfront (1954) was originally turned down by a number of studios because, as Hollywood mogul Darryl Zanuck commented at the time: "Who gives a shit about labor unions?" In that movie, the villains are the corrupt union leaders.
Ch. Blue-Collar Blues
Body Snatchers, la paranoia anticomunista

In Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1956, 1978), plant pods from another world take possession of our bodies and convert us into obedient automatons. When the heroes try to sound the alarm, they discover that the authorities themselves have been invaded by the pods.
Ch. Swarthy Hordes and Other Aliens
The Green Berets, propaganda del Pentágono

The military assisted in every conceivable way in filming The Green Berets (1968), a story of how Special Forces killer John Wayne guns down hordes of Vietnamese just as he did Indians and Japanese in earlier flicks, thereby seeming to win the Vietnam war.
Ch. The Media Fight the Red Menace
Dirty Harry inaugura al policía vigilante

A number of movies appearing in the 1970s and 1980s featured rogue cops like Clint Eastwood's Dirty Harry (1971), and its sequels. Magnum Force (1973), The Enforcer (1976), Sudden Impact (1983), and The Dead Pool (1988).
Ch. Affluent Class and Corporate Brass
Star Wars y la cosmologia individualista

In another series of motion pictures. Star Wars (1977), The Empire Strikes Back (1980), and Return of the Jedi (1983), the subject is an evil cosmic power that is challenged by individualistic heroes. The heroes are obediently assisted by robots and "lower" nonhuman creatures from other planets.

Blue Collar criminaliza al sindicato

Likewise, in Blue Collar (1978), the union is an undemocratic instrument of corruption, coercion, and terror within the Detroit automotive industry, murdering one of its own rank-and-file members and buying off another, pitting older workers against young, Black against White.

Missing in Action, revancha en Vietnam

Missing in Action (1984). Chuck Norris escapes from a Vietnamese prisoner-of-war camp years after the war. He then returns to Vietnam with a sidekick to liberate the other MIA-POWs from the clutches of the sadistic Vietnamese, who cackle a lot and simply cannot shoot

In both Top Gun (1986), a film about young bucks at an elite naval aviation training school who vie for macho glory, and The Hunt for Red October (1990), about a diabolic Soviet submarine commander, the U.S. Navy cooperated fully, providing the jet-fighter planes

Wall Street, los límites del cine liberal

Special attention should be given to Oliver Stone's Wall Street (1987). Though a good film, it illustrates better than most "antibusiness" movies the limits of a liberal critique. The main character, inside trader and cutthroat corporate raider Gordon Gekko (Michael Douglas) represents bad Wall Street.
